content: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is known to cause secondary infections in individuals with eczema and may exacerbate inflammation even in cases where the eczema does not appear to be infected. Currently, there is no standardized approach to reducing the burden of S. aureus in eczema management. It remains uncertain whether antimicrobial treatments are beneficial for eczema or if they contribute to the development of bacterial resistance. This study is an update of a 2008 Cochrane Review and aims to evaluate the effects of interventions targeting S. aureus in the treatment of eczema. The review included 41 randomized controlled trials involving 1,753 participants, covering 10 different treatment categories. These studies were conducted primarily in secondary care settings across Western Europe, North America, the Far East, and other regions. Participants ranged in age from 1.1 to 34.6 years, with eczema severity varying from mild to severe. However, many studies did not report key outcomes such as global improvement in symptoms, quality of life (QOL), or adverse events. Treatment durations ranged from 10 minutes to 3 months, while total study durations spanned 15 weeks to 27 months. A significant number of studies (33 out of 41) were assessed as having a high risk of bias in at least one domain. Topical Steroid/Antibiotic Combinations vs. Topical Steroids Alone Fourteen studies compared the use of topical steroid/antibiotic combinations to topical steroids alone. These studies included participants with infected eczema (2 studies), uninfected eczema (4 studies), and unspecified infective status (8 studies). Evidence suggests that topical steroid/antibiotic combinations may result in slightly greater global improvement in eczema symptoms compared to topical steroids alone at 6 to 28 days of follow-up (risk ratio [RR] 1.10, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00 to 1.21; 224 participants; 3 studies, low-quality evidence). However, there was likely little to no difference in QOL outcomes for children at 14 days of follow-up (mean difference [MD] -0.18, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.04; 42 participants; 1 study, moderate-quality evidence). Severe adverse events were rare but included dermatitis flares, worsening eczema, and folliculitis, with similar occurrences in both groups (325 participants; 4 studies, very low-quality evidence). Minor adverse events, such as stinging, itching, and folliculitis, were less frequent in the combination group at 14 days of follow-up (218 participants; 2 studies). One study reported antibiotic resistance in children at 3 months of follow-up, with no significant differences between the groups (65 participants; 1 study). Oral Antibiotics vs. Placebo Four studies evaluated the use of oral antibiotics compared to placebo. These studies included participants with infected eczema (2 studies), uninfected eczema (1 study), and colonized but clinically uninfected eczema (1 study). Oral antibiotics may not provide significant benefits in terms of global improvement in eczema symptoms for infants and children at 14 to 28 days of follow-up compared to placebo (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.18 to 3.50; 75 participants; 2 studies, low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was likely little to no difference in QOL outcomes at 14 days of follow-up (MD 0.11, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.32; 45 participants; 1 study, moderate-quality evidence). Adverse events requiring treatment withdrawal were rare but included worsening eczema (both groups), loose stools (antibiotic group), and Henoch-Schönlein purpura (placebo group) (4 studies, 199 participants, very low-quality evidence). Minor adverse events, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and joint pain, were infrequent and generally low in both groups (1 study, 68 participants). Antibiotic resistance at 14 days was reported as similar between the groups (2 studies, 98 participants). Bleach Baths vs. Placebo or Bath Emollients Five studies assessed the effects of bleach baths compared to placebo (water) or bath emollients. One study reported global improvement and found that bleach baths may not differ significantly from placebo in terms of symptom improvement at 1 month of follow-up (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.63; 36 participants; low-quality evidence). Another study indicated that there was likely little to no difference in QOL outcomes at 28 days of follow-up (MD 0.90, 95% CI -1.32 to 3.12; 80 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Adverse events leading to treatment withdrawal were rare, with one participant in the placebo group discontinuing due to worsening itch (1 study, 42 participants, very low-quality evidence). Minor adverse events, such as burning, stinging, or dry skin, were reported in both groups, with no significant differences (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.87; 36 participants; low-quality evidence). Antibiotic resistance at 4 weeks of follow-up was also uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (1 study, 80 participants). Authors' Conclusions The evidence regarding the effects of anti-staphylococcal treatments for managing infected or uninfected eczema remains insufficient. The quality of evidence was generally low due to risks of bias, imprecise effect estimates, and heterogeneity among studies. Topical steroid/antibiotic combinations may offer small improvements in eczema symptoms compared to topical steroids alone, but high-quality trials are needed to better evaluate their efficacy, impact on QOL, and potential for antibiotic resistance.
